---
title: "Activity 3: meta-regression and publication bias"
---

::: {.session-banner .practical}
**Activity.** We continue with the simulated warming dataset (lnRR). Do sex and body size explain why effects differ? And is there evidence of publication bias? Try each step before opening the 💡 *Solution* boxes.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(tidyverse,   # data handling and plots
               metafor,     # meta-analysis
               orchaRd,     # orchard and bubble plots, I2, R2
               ape,         # phylogenetic trees
               patchwork)   # put ggplots side by side

# Workshop colours and plot style
source(here::here("R", "theme_workshop.R"))
```

# Prepare the data, V and A (as in Activity 2)

Run this chunk. It repeats the preparation from [Activity 2](activity-2-multilevel.qmd) (lnRR, the shared-control matrix **V** and the phylogenetic matrix **A**) and adds the new columns we need here:

- `log_mass_c`: log~10~ body mass, **centred** (the average species has value 0). Centring makes the intercept mean "an animal of average size".
- `inv_sqrt_n`: $\sqrt{1/\tilde{n}}$, where $\tilde{n} = N_{1}N_{2} / (N_{1} + N_{2})$ is the 'effective sample size' (group 1 = treatment, group 2 = control). It measures how imprecise a study is, and we'll use it to test for small-study effects.
- `year_c`: publication year, centred on the average year.

```{r}
#| label: prep
# Read in the simulated contrast data
contrast_dat <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sim_contrast.csv"))

# lnRR and its sampling variance
contrast_es <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                      m1i = treatment_mean,     # group 1 = treatment
                      sd1i = treatment_sd,
                      n1i = treatment_n,
                      m2i = control_mean,       # group 2 = control
                      sd2i = control_sd,
                      n2i = control_n,
                      data = contrast_dat)

contrast_es$es_ID <- 1:nrow(contrast_es)       # one ID per effect size
contrast_es$phylo <- contrast_es$species       # copy of species for the phylogenetic effect

# Moderators
contrast_es$sex        <- factor(contrast_es$sex, levels = c("female", "male"))   # female = reference
contrast_es$log_mass   <- log10(contrast_es$body_size)
contrast_es$log_mass_c <- contrast_es$log_mass - mean(contrast_es$log_mass)       # centred

# Publication-bias moderators
contrast_es$n_tilde    <- (contrast_es$treatment_n * contrast_es$control_n) /
                          (contrast_es$treatment_n + contrast_es$control_n)       # effective sample size
contrast_es$inv_sqrt_n <- sqrt(1 / contrast_es$n_tilde)
contrast_es$year_c     <- contrast_es$study_year - mean(contrast_es$study_year)   # centred year

# Shared-control V matrix (same as Activity 2)
contrast_es$cov_c <- contrast_es$control_sd^2 /
  (contrast_es$control_n * contrast_es$control_mean^2)

k <- nrow(contrast_es)
V <- diag(contrast_es$vi)
for (i in 1:k) {
  for (j in 1:k) {
    if (i != j & contrast_es$comparison_ID[i] == contrast_es$comparison_ID[j]) {
      V[i, j] <- contrast_es$cov_c[i]
    }
  }
}

# Phylogenetic correlation matrix (same as Activity 2)
tree <- read.tree(here::here("data", "sim_tree.tre"))
tree <- keep.tip(tree, unique(contrast_es$species))
A <- vcv(tree, corr = TRUE)
```

---

# Task 1 – Model 1 (Model 2 from Activity 2)

**Goal:** re-create the final model from Activity 2. It is the starting point and comparison model for this activity.

**What to do:** fit `rma.mv()` with the matrix `V`, the four random effects (`study_ID`, `es_ID`, `species`, `phylo`) and `R = list(phylo = A)`, plus `test = "t"` and `dfs = "contain"`. Save it as `model1`. Your estimate should match Model 2 from Activity 2.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Solution
```{r}
#| label: model1
model1 <- rma.mv(yi = yi,
                 V = V,                         # shared-control V matrix
                 random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                               ~ 1 | es_ID,
                               ~ 1 | species,
                               ~ 1 | phylo),
                 R = list(phylo = A),           # phylogenetic correlation matrix
                 test = "t",
                 dfs = "contain",
                 data = contrast_es)

summary(model1)
```
:::

---

# Task 2 – Meta-regression with sex and body size (Model 2)

**Goal:** test whether **sex** and **body size** explain why the effect of warming differs among effect sizes.

**What to do:**

1. **Look at the data first.**
   - Count effect sizes per sex with `contrast_es %>% count(sex)`.
   - Make a boxplot of `yi` by `sex`, and a scatterplot of `yi` against `log_mass`. Do you expect an effect of either?
2. **Fit the model.** Copy Model 1 and add `mods = ~ sex + log_mass_c`. Save it as `model2`.
3. **Read the *Model Results* table:**
   - `intrcpt`: the expected lnRR for the reference group (**females**) of **average** body mass;
   - `sexmale`: how much **higher or lower** males are than females (a difference, not the male mean);
   - `log_mass_c`: change in lnRR for a 10-fold increase in body mass.
4. **How much heterogeneity do the moderators explain?** Use `r2_ml(model2)`. `R2_marginal` is the proportion explained by sex and body size.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Solution
```{r}
#| label: explore
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
# 1. Look at the data
contrast_es %>%
  count(sex)

# Boxplot of lnRR by sex
p1 <- ggplot(contrast_es, aes(x = sex, y = yi)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#fecdd0", outlier.shape = NA) +   # hide outlier dots (all points are drawn below)
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = pal["red"]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "lnRR")

# Scatterplot of lnRR against body mass
p2 <- ggplot(contrast_es, aes(x = log_mass, y = yi)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = pal["red"]) +
  labs(x = "log10 body mass (g)", y = "lnRR")

p1 + p2
```

```{r}
#| label: model2
# 2. Fit the meta-regression
model2 <- rma.mv(yi = yi,
                 V = V,
                 mods = ~ sex + log_mass_c,     # the two moderators
                 random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                               ~ 1 | es_ID,
                               ~ 1 | species,
                               ~ 1 | phylo),
                 R = list(phylo = A),
                 test = "t",
                 dfs = "contain",
                 data = contrast_es)

summary(model2)

# 4. Variance explained by the moderators
r2_ml(model2)
```

**Interpretation**

- `intrcpt` = expected lnRR for **females** of **average body mass**: `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[1])` (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (exp(model2$b[1]) - 1))`%).
- `sexmale` = difference between males and females: `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[2])` (*p* `r fmt_p(model2$pval[2])`). Males respond `r if_else(model2$b[2] > 0, "more", "less")` strongly to warming.
- `log_mass_c` = change in lnRR per 10-fold increase in body mass: `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[3])` (*p* `r fmt_p(model2$pval[3])`).
- The true values used in the simulation (`data/sim_truth.csv`) were +0.12 for males and −0.08 per log~10~ g.
:::

---

# Task 3 – Orchard plot of Model 2 with a moderator

**Goal:** visualise the effect of sex (and, optionally, body size).

**What to do:**

1. Make an orchard plot by sex: `orchard_plot(model2, mod = "sex", group = "study_ID", xlab = "lnRR")`. You get one 'branch' per sex. Because the model also contains body size, each sex mean is calculated for an animal of average body size.
2. Compare the female and male means and their CIs. Do the CIs overlap much?
3. **Optional:** body size is continuous, so use a **bubble plot** instead: `bubble_plot(model2, mod = "log_mass_c", group = "study_ID")`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Solution
```{r}
#| label: fig-orchard-sex
#| fig-cap: "Orchard plot of Model 2 for sex: mean lnRR for females and males (circles), 95% CIs (thick bars) and prediction intervals (thin bars). k = effect sizes (studies)."
#| fig-height: 4
orchard_plot(model2,
             mod = "sex",              # one 'branch' per sex
             group = "study_ID",       # count the number of studies
             xlab = "lnRR (warming vs control)",
             cb = FALSE)               # use the workshop's red colours
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bubble-mass
#| fig-cap: "Bubble plot of Model 2 for body mass (averaged over sex)."
#| fig-height: 4
bubble_plot(model2,
            mod = "log_mass_c",        # the continuous moderator
            group = "study_ID",
            xlab = "log10 body mass (centred)",
            ylab = "lnRR",
            legend.pos = "top.right",
            est.col = "#e12744")       # colour of the regression line
```
:::

---

# Task 4 – Small-study and time-lag effects (Model 3)

**Goal:** check for signs of **publication bias**.

- **Small-study effect:** small (imprecise) studies report larger effects, possibly because small studies with 'boring' results were never published.
- **Time-lag (decline) effect:** effects get smaller over time, as early exciting results are followed by more cautious ones.

**What to do:**

1. **Funnel plot.** Run `funnel(x = contrast_es$yi, vi = contrast_es$vi, yaxis = "seinv")`. Without bias the points form a symmetric funnel. Are there 'missing' points at the bottom (imprecise studies) on one side?
2. **Fit Model 3.** Copy Model 2 and add the two bias moderators: `mods = ~ sex + log_mass_c + inv_sqrt_n + year_c`. Save it as `model3`.
3. **Read the two new rows:**
   - a **positive** `inv_sqrt_n` slope means less precise studies report larger effects (a small-study effect);
   - a **negative** `year_c` slope means effects decline over time.
4. **Optional:** draw a bubble plot for each with `bubble_plot(model3, mod = "inv_sqrt_n", group = "study_ID")` and `mod = "year_c"`.

*Why `inv_sqrt_n` and not the standard error of lnRR?* The SE of lnRR is calculated from the means themselves, so it is partly linked to the effect size even without any bias. $\sqrt{1/\tilde{n}}$ depends only on sample size.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Solution
```{r}
#| label: fig-funnel
#| fig-cap: "Funnel plot of lnRR against precision (1/SE)."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 6
funnel(x = contrast_es$yi,        # effect sizes
       vi = contrast_es$vi,       # sampling variances
       yaxis = "seinv",           # y-axis = precision (1 / SE)
       col = "#e12744",           # colour of the points
       xlab = "lnRR",
       ylab = "Precision (1/SE)")
```

```{r}
#| label: model3
model3 <- rma.mv(yi = yi,
                 V = V,
                 mods = ~ sex + log_mass_c + inv_sqrt_n + year_c,   # + two bias moderators
                 random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                               ~ 1 | es_ID,
                               ~ 1 | species,
                               ~ 1 | phylo),
                 R = list(phylo = A),
                 test = "t",
                 dfs = "contain",
                 data = contrast_es)

summary(model3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias
#| fig-cap: "Small-study (left) and time-lag (right) effects from Model 3."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 10
# Small-study effect
p_small <- bubble_plot(model3,
                       mod = "inv_sqrt_n",
                       group = "study_ID",
                       xlab = "sqrt(1 / effective n)",
                       ylab = "lnRR",
                       legend.pos = "none",
                       est.col = "#e12744")

# Time-lag effect
p_year <- bubble_plot(model3,
                      mod = "year_c",
                      group = "study_ID",
                      xlab = "Publication year (centred)",
                      ylab = "lnRR",
                      legend.pos = "none",
                      est.col = "#e12744")

p_small + p_year   # side by side with patchwork
```
:::

---

# Task 5 – How do the results differ?

**Goal:** see what changes when publication bias is taken into account.

**What to do:**

1. Put the coefficient tables of Model 2 and Model 3 side by side: `coef(summary(model2))` and `coef(summary(model3))`.
2. For **sex** and **body size**: did the estimates change much?
3. For the **intercept**: did it change? What does the intercept of Model 3 represent? (Think about what `inv_sqrt_n = 0` and `year_c = 0` mean.)
4. Did the marginal $R^2$ (`r2_ml()`) change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Solution
```{r}
#| label: compare
# Coefficient tables (estimate, se, tval, df, pval, ci.lb, ci.ub)
round(coef(summary(model2)), 4)
round(coef(summary(model3)), 4)

# Variance explained by the moderators
r2_ml(model2)
r2_ml(model3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients (± 95% CI) of Models 2 and 3. The intercept drops sharply once the small-study and time-lag effects are included."
#| fig-height: 3.6
# Put both coefficient tables into one data frame for plotting
coef_2 <- data.frame(model = "Model 2",
                     term = rownames(coef(summary(model2))),
                     coef(summary(model2)))

coef_3 <- data.frame(model = "Model 3",
                     term = rownames(coef(summary(model3))),
                     coef(summary(model3)))

coef_tbl <- rbind(coef_2, coef_3)   # stack the two tables

ggplot(coef_tbl, aes(x = estimate, y = term, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci.lb, xmax = ci.ub), width = 0.2, orientation = "y",
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("dark", "red")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (lnRR scale)", y = NULL)
```

**What changed?**

- **Sex and body size:** the male–female difference is essentially unchanged (`r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[2])` → `r sprintf("%.3f", model3$b[2])`), so these moderators are robust to the bias adjustment.
- **Small-study effect:** positive slope for `inv_sqrt_n` (`r sprintf("%.2f", model3$b[4])`, *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[4])`). Less precise studies report larger increases, which is the signature of selective publication.
- **Time-lag effect:** negative slope for `year_c` (`r sprintf("%.4f", model3$b[5])` per year, *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[5])`). Effects reported in early studies were larger.
- **The intercept** falls from `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", model3$b[1])`. It now estimates the effect for an infinitely large study (`inv_sqrt_n = 0`), published in the average year (`year_c = 0`), on females of average size. The 'average' effect of warming in Model 2 was partly inflated by publication bias.
- **Caveat:** the intercept of Model 3 extrapolates to `inv_sqrt_n = 0`, well outside the observed data, so its CI is wide and it tends to *over*-correct. In the simulation the true female effect for an average year is about 0.15–0.20, so the bias-corrected intercept is too low. Treat bias-corrected estimates as a **sensitivity analysis**, not as 'the true effect'.
:::

---

# Task 6 – Write a results section for Model 3

**Goal:** report the full analysis in three short paragraphs.

**What to do:** write one paragraph for each of:

1. **Overall effect and heterogeneity** (from Model 1): *k*, studies and species; lnRR with 95% CI and *p*; the % change; $I^2_{total}$ and how it splits (`i2_ml(model1)`); the prediction interval (`predict(model1)`).
2. **Moderators** (from Model 2): the sex difference and the body-size slope, each with its estimate, 95% CI and *p*; the marginal $R^2$.
3. **Publication bias** (from Model 3): the small-study and time-lag slopes with 95% CI and *p*; whether sex and body size changed; the bias-adjusted intercept and how it compares with the unadjusted mean.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 💡 Example write-up

```{r}
#| label: writeup-values
# Values used in the write-up
i2_m1   <- i2_ml(model1)       # I2 of Model 1
pred_m1 <- predict(model1)     # mean, CI and prediction interval of Model 1

# A small function to convert lnRR to a % change (as text)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (exp(x) - 1))
```

::: {.writeup}
**Overall effect and heterogeneity.** Across `r model1$k` effect sizes from `r length(unique(contrast_es$study_ID))` studies of `r length(unique(contrast_es$species))` vertebrate species, experimental warming increased physiological rates by `r pct(model1$b[1])`% (lnRR = `r sprintf("%.3f", model1$b[1])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", model1$ci.lb)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", model1$ci.ub)`; *p* `r fmt_p(model1$pval)`). Heterogeneity was high ($I^2_{total}$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", i2_m1[1])`%; phylogeny `r sprintf("%.1f", i2_m1["I2_phylo"])`%, species `r sprintf("%.1f", i2_m1["I2_species"])`%, study `r sprintf("%.1f", i2_m1["I2_study_ID"])`%, effect size `r sprintf("%.1f", i2_m1["I2_es_ID"])`%), and the 95% prediction interval spanned `r pct(pred_m1$pi.lb)`% to `r pct(pred_m1$pi.ub)`%.

**Moderators.** In a meta-regression including sex and body mass (Model 2; $R^2_{marginal}$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r2_ml(model2)[1])`%), males showed a larger response to warming than females (difference in lnRR = `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[2])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$ci.lb[2])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$ci.ub[2])`; *p* `r fmt_p(model2$pval[2])`; Fig. 3), and the response `r if_else(model2$b[3] < 0, "decreased", "increased")` with body mass (slope = `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$b[3])` per log~10~ g, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$ci.lb[3])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", model2$ci.ub[3])`; *p* `r fmt_p(model2$pval[3])`).

**Publication bias.** When effective sample size and publication year were added (Model 3), we found evidence of a small-study effect (slope for √(1/ñ) = `r sprintf("%.2f", model3$b[4])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f", model3$ci.lb[4])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", model3$ci.ub[4])`; *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[4])`) and a decline in effect sizes over time (slope = `r sprintf("%.4f", model3$b[5])` per year, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.4f", model3$ci.lb[5])` to `r sprintf("%.4f", model3$ci.ub[5])`; *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[5])`). The effects of sex (`r sprintf("%.3f", model3$b[2])`, *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[2])`) and body mass (`r sprintf("%.3f", model3$b[3])`, *p* `r fmt_p(model3$pval[3])`) were robust to these adjustments. However, the bias-adjusted intercept (lnRR = `r sprintf("%.3f", model3$b[1])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", model3$ci.lb[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", model3$ci.ub[1])`) was much smaller than the unadjusted estimate, indicating that the magnitude of the overall effect of warming is likely overestimated in the published literature.
:::
:::
